summary_for_principal:
A governed process can now genuinely call an outside service, not just run its own code or hand work to a person.

This was previously refused outright, alongside one other kind (composing several small tools together, still refused, coming next). The design doc had judged the gap unclear; re-reading the format's own written rules found the answer was already there, unconnected. Now closed: an external call runs with the same discipline as internal code — checked, retried on temporary failure, recorded — kept visibly distinct from it, not blurred together.

Building this meant threading the new capability through every place the system builds its own working context, since it's one of the small set every governed run needs. Mechanical, done everywhere at once.

Full test suite: 448 passed. Lint, formatting and type checks all clean.

Numbered actions:
1. Nothing needs deciding — built, tested, ready to merge when CI is green.
2. Next up: composing several small tools together as one unit.

filled_in.gap: The design document named 'the exact same shape as CodeToolPort... the same ToolTransientError/ToolPermanentError pair' without specifying whether that meant a second, parallel pair of exception classes defined in external_tool.py, or the literal same classes imported from code_tool.py.
filled_in.assumed: Reuse code_tool.py's own ToolTransientError/ToolPermanentError classes verbatim (import, don't redefine) — both dispatch kinds classify a failure by the identical mechanism (the Tool's own declared errors[], spec §4.6), so a second, structurally identical pair would be pure duplication; attempt_step's own error-handling code catches one pair regardless of which port raised it, which a duplicate pair would have broken (two except clauses, or an isinstance check).
filled_in.grounded_in: CLAUDE.md's 'no half-finished implementations' and general minimal-duplication discipline — the design's own reasoning for keeping ExternalToolPort itself distinct (a real compliance-bar difference) does not extend to the exception classes, which carry no dispatch-kind-specific meaning.
filled_in.reversal_cost: Low — a future pass that needs EXTERNAL-specific exception behaviour can add a distinct pair without touching CODE's own.

filled_in.gap: Extending EngineContext with a new required field (external_tool, no default, matching every other port field's own convention) meant every existing EngineContext(...) construction site across the test suite needed updating — 49 call sites across 4 files, 46 of them in tests/engine/test_run.py alone.
filled_in.assumed: Update every call site (via a small parsing script that finds each EngineContext(...) call's own code_tool= argument and inserts external_tool=StubExternalToolAdapter() right after it) rather than giving external_tool a default value to avoid the churn. Consistency with every other port field (policy/code_tool/records/claims/registry/identity/platform_id all lack defaults; only lease_seconds, a host SETTING not a port, has one) was judged worth the mechanical diff, especially since a caller silently getting a default 'do-nothing' external adapter it never asked for is a worse failure mode than being forced to supply one explicitly.
filled_in.grounded_in: CLAUDE.md's 'fail closed' — EngineContext's own existing pattern (every port mandatory) is itself already an expression of that principle; breaking it for one field to save test-file churn would have been inconsistent with the pattern this exact PR is extending.
filled_in.reversal_cost: Low — giving external_tool a default later is a pure loosening, breaking nothing currently passing.

decisions.headline: D44 — mechanism.kind: EXTERNAL is now dispatched by the engine, closing the EXTERNAL half of D34: a new ExternalToolPort, mirroring CodeToolPort's own shape exactly, is wired into attempt_step alongside CodeToolPort, sharing every surrounding rule.
decisions.problem: D34 refused both EXTERNAL and TOOL (composite) together, reasoning EXTERNAL needed a new domain port whose shape the spec did not describe ('per adapter' names no operational contract). Re-reading spec §4.3 directly found that reasoning had already been answered: EXTERNAL's own contract (an opaque adapter id, checked by the adapter's own contract tests) is the same SHAPE CODE already has, differing only in what the ref names.
options_rejected: Reuse CodeToolPort itself for EXTERNAL dispatch rather than a second port: rejected — the compliance bar genuinely differs (CODE's contract is exercisable by this engine's own tests; EXTERNAL's is entirely the host adapter's own), a boundary worth keeping visible in the type system.

Give EXTERNAL its own parallel ToolTransientError/ToolPermanentError pair: rejected — both dispatch kinds classify failures identically (the Tool's own declared errors[]), so reusing code_tool.py's own pair verbatim avoids pure duplication.

Duplicate attempt_step's own surrounding logic (permission, precondition, inputs, controls) in engine/run.py for a separate EXTERNAL-only dispatch path: rejected — steps.py's own module docstring already named extending attempt_step as 'a later step' for exactly this reason.
decisions.cost_to_change: Low — ExternalToolPort/StubExternalToolAdapter are additive; attempt_step's own dispatch-kind branch and _advance_step's narrowed condition are both small, local changes with no schema or durable-record shape change.
